questions.q: When you use Remove Duplicates, what determines which rows count as duplicates of each other?
options: The specific column or columns you select before running the command
Power Query always compares every column in the table automatically
Only the first column in the table is ever checked
Duplicates are removed randomly
questions.explain: Selecting just an ID column defines uniqueness differently than selecting ID + date — the columns you select before running Remove Duplicates decide what 'duplicate' means for that run.

questions.q: What does Split Column by Delimiter do?
options: Breaks one text column into multiple columns using a chosen separator character
Deletes the selected column entirely
Merges two columns into one
Sorts the column alphabetically
questions.explain: Splitting by delimiter (comma, hyphen, space, or custom) turns one column packed with multiple pieces of information into several clean columns, named with a .1, .2 suffix by default.

questions.q: Why does getting a column's data type right matter?
options: Sorts, filters, date math, and merges downstream all depend on Power Query knowing what kind of value is actually in that column
It only affects the color of the column header
Data types are purely cosmetic and don't affect anything else
It's required only for the very last column in a table
questions.explain: A wrong type — like ZIP codes loaded as a number, silently dropping a leading zero — quietly breaks later steps that assume a different type, which is why fixing types early in a query matters.

questions.q: How do you filter out blank rows in Power Query?
options: Use the same per-column filter dropdown and uncheck the (blank) entry, just like any other unwanted value
There is no way to filter blank rows in Power Query
You must delete them manually from the source file first
Blank rows are removed automatically with no user action
questions.explain: Blank/null values appear in the filter dropdown's value list as an explicit (blank) entry — unchecking it filters those rows out, and because it's a recorded step, it survives a refresh.

questions.q: Why does a filter step (unlike a manual row delete) keep working after the query is refreshed with new data?
options: Because it's recorded as an Applied Step that re-runs against whatever data comes in on the next refresh
Because filters are stored in the original source file
It doesn't — filters have to be re-applied by hand every time
Because Power Query ignores refreshes entirely
questions.explain: Every cleaning operation in this lesson becomes a step in Applied Steps, and Refresh re-runs every step — including filters — against the current data, not just the data you first loaded.
